lesson.title: How Tightly Are They Linked: Quantifying Magnetic Coupling
lesson.summary: The coupling coefficient k rescales mutual inductance into a unitless number between 0 and 1, answering the practical question of just how much of one coil's magnetic field actually reaches the other.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter's mutual inductance value of 12 millihenries is hard to judge on its own. Is that tight coupling or loose coupling between the two coils? The answer depends on how large L1 and L2 are to begin with, since a bigger pair of coils can support a bigger M even with mediocre alignment. What is needed is a normalized number that strips out the size of the coils and leaves only the sharing efficiency, which is exactly what the coupling coefficient provides.

The coupling coefficient is defined as k = M divided by the square root of L1 times L2. It is unitless by construction, and it always falls between 0 and 1. A value of k = 0 means none of coil one's flux reaches coil two, no coupling at all. A value of k = 1 means every bit of flux produced by one coil passes through the other, the theoretical maximum, approached in practice by coils wound tightly together on a shared iron core, as in a well built power transformer. Loosely spaced air core coils, or the coils in a wireless phone charger separated by a plastic case, typically sit much lower, often k = 0.1 to 0.5 depending on alignment and gap.

Worked example: take the same transformer from the mutual inductance chapter, with L1 = 10 millihenries, L2 = 40 millihenries, and measured M = 12 millihenries. Then k = M divided by the square root of L1 times L2 = 0.012 divided by the square root of 0.01 times 0.04. Multiplying inside the root gives 0.0004, and the square root of 0.0004 is 0.02. So k = 0.012 divided by 0.02 = 0.6. A coupling coefficient of 0.6 describes moderate coupling: a real, usable magnetic link, but well short of the near perfect sharing you would get from a tightly wound shared core.

It is worth noting that k also sets a hard ceiling on M itself. Since k can never exceed 1, M can never be larger than the square root of L1 times L2, about 0.02 henries, or 20 millihenries, for this coil pair. If a lab measurement ever produced an M bigger than that limit, it would be a clear sign of a measurement or calculation error, not a real physical result.

The coupling coefficient matters well beyond bookkeeping. The portion of energy that does not couple across, represented by 1 minus k, shows up as leakage inductance, energy that sloshes back and forth in one coil's own field without ever reaching the other side. In wireless power transfer and switch mode transformer design, a low k means real efficiency losses and design headaches, which is why engineers work hard to push k as close to 1 as the physical geometry allows.

Physical construction is really the whole story behind k. Winding both coils on a shared laminated iron or ferrite core gives the magnetic field a low resistance path that keeps almost all of it contained and shared between windings, pushing k up toward 0.95 or higher in a well built power transformer. Air core coils have no such path, the field spreads freely into open space in every direction, so only a fraction of it happens to pass through the second coil, which is why loosely coupled air core designs, like the coils in some wireless chargers or radio frequency identification readers, often operate with k values well under 0.5 and still have to be engineered carefully around that limitation.
